questions.stem: For a dialysis membrane, about the solvent fluxes:
options: The diffusive flux of solvent is J_d = LΔπ
The convective flux of solvent is J_c = LΔP
The net solvent flux is the vector sum J_net = J_c + J_d
The convective flux of solvent is J_c = P|ΔC|
The net solvent flux carries no solute across the membrane
questions.explanation: For the solvent, J_d = LΔπ and J_c = LΔP, and J_net = J_c + J_d. P|ΔC| is the diffusive flux of the solute, not of the solvent, and J_net does carry a solute flux along with it (J_cs = J_net·C̄s).

questions.stem: Across a dialysis membrane, the convective flux of solute J_cs carried by the net solvent flux:
options: Is J_cs = J_net·C̄s
Uses C̄s = the concentration of the more concentrated compartment
Uses C̄s = (C₁s + C₂s) / 2
Is J_cs = P|ΔCs|
Is not zero when C₁s = C₂s, provided J_net ≠ 0
questions.explanation: J_cs = J_net·C̄s with C̄s the mean of the two concentrations, so it exists whenever solvent flows, even with no concentration difference. P|ΔCs| is the diffusive solute flux, which does vanish when ΔCs = 0.

questions.stem: A dialysis membrane separates two solutions of a solute at C₁ = 12 mmol/L and C₂ = 8 mmol/L. The net solvent flux is J_net = 2×10⁻⁸ m/s. The convective flux of solute J_cs (in mol·m⁻²·s⁻¹) is:
questions.explanation: J_cs = J_net·C̄s with C̄s = (12 + 8)/2 = 10 mmol/L = 10 mol/m³, so J_cs = 2×10⁻⁸ × 10 = 2×10⁻⁷. Using ΔC = 4 gives 8×10⁻⁸ (that is the wrong concentration), and the sum 20 gives 4×10⁻⁷.
questions.mental: 1 mmol/L = 1 mol/m³, so C̄s = 10 mol/m³; 2×10⁻⁸ × 10 = 2×10⁻⁷. 2×10⁻¹⁰ comes from leaving C̄s in mol/L (0.01), and 2×10⁻⁵ is 100× too big — a powers-of-ten check removes both.

questions.stem: For a biological membrane, whose selectivity is described by the reflection coefficient σ:
options: The diffusive flux of solvent is J_d = LσΔπ
The convective flux of solvent is J_c = LσΔP
Darcy's law of filtration gives J_c = (P_f·V_me / RT)·ΔP
L = P_f·V_me / RT
The filtration coefficient P_f is expressed in m²·s/kg
questions.explanation: Only the diffusive (osmotic) solvent flux carries σ: J_d = LσΔπ, while J_c = LΔP (Darcy's law, with L = P_fV_me/RT). P_f is in m/s; m²·s/kg is the unit of L.

questions.stem: About Darcy's law of filtration J_c = (P_f·V_me / RT)·ΔP:
options: V_me is the molar volume of water, V_me = 18 cm³
P_f is the membrane filtration coefficient, in m/s
V_me is the molar volume of the solute
J_c is proportional to the temperature T
J_c increases when the pressure difference ΔP increases
questions.explanation: V_me is the molar volume of water (18 cm³), P_f the filtration coefficient in m/s, and J_c is proportional to ΔP. T is in the denominator, so J_c is inversely, not directly, proportional to T.

questions.stem: Across a biological membrane, the convective solute flux is J_cs = (1 − σ)·J_net·C̄s. Therefore:
options: (1 − σ) is the membrane transmission coefficient
σ is the membrane transmission coefficient
For a solute to which the membrane is impermeable (σ = 1), J_cs = 0
For σ = 0, the expression becomes that of the dialysis membrane, J_cs = J_net·C̄s
The net solute flux is the vector sum of J_cs and the diffusive flux J_ds = P|ΔCs|
questions.explanation: σ is the reflection coefficient and (1 − σ) the transmission coefficient: σ = 1 stops all convective transport of the solute, σ = 0 gives back J_cs = J_net·C̄s. The net solute flux is J_cs + J_ds.

questions.stem: A capillary membrane is impermeable to albumin but lets glucose and other small molecules through. About its reflection coefficients:
options: σ (albumin) = 1
σ (albumin) = 0
σ (glucose) = 0
σ (glucose) = 1
The transmission coefficient for albumin is 1
questions.explanation: A solute that cannot cross is fully reflected (σ = 1); a freely crossing one has σ = 0. The transmission coefficient for albumin is 1 − σ = 0, not 1.

questions.stem: A capillary membrane is impermeable to albumin (M = 40 000 g/mol). Plasma contains 40 g/L of albumin and the interstitial medium none. At 37 °C (R = 8.31 SI), the osmotic pressure difference generated by albumin is about:
options: 2.6 kPa (≈ 19 mmHg)
2.6 Pa
9.7 mmHg
2.6 MPa
39 mmHg
questions.explanation: Δπ = ω·RT = (40/40 000 mol/L = 1 mol/m³) × 8.31 × 310 ≈ 2 576 Pa ≈ 19.4 mmHg (1 mmHg = 133 Pa). 9.7 mmHg is the value for 20 g/L in the lesson's exercise; 2.6 Pa comes from leaving ω in mol/L.
questions.mental: 40/40 000 = 10⁻³ mol/L = 1 mol/m³, so Δπ = RT ≈ 8.3 × 310 ≈ 2 600 Pa; ÷133 ≈ 20 mmHg. The Pa and MPa options are off by 10³ — a unit check removes them; 9.7 is half, i.e. the 20 g/L case.

options: It describes water exchange between plasma and the interstitial medium
The capillary wall is modeled as a dialysis membrane
P_a is the blood pressure at the exit (venular end) of the capillary
P_int is the pressure in the interstitial medium
ΔP_v = P_v − P_int
questions.explanation: Starling describes plasma ↔ interstitial water exchange through a capillary wall treated as a dialysis membrane. P_a is the pressure at the entrance (arteriolar end) and P_v at the exit, with P_a > P_v.

questions.stem: In the Starling model, the osmotic pressure difference Δπ between plasma and the interstitial medium:
options: Is due to the plasma proteins, since ω_int ≈ ω_i
Equals (ω_i + ω_p)·RT
Equals ω_p·RT
Draws water from the interstitial medium toward the plasma
Draws water from the plasma toward the interstitial medium
questions.explanation: ω_plasma = ω_i + ω_p and ω_int ≈ ω_i, so Δπ = (ω_plasma − ω_int)RT = ω_p·RT, due to the proteins only. Δπ acts from the interstitial medium toward the plasma; it is ΔP that pushes water out of the plasma.

questions.stem: Under normal conditions, in the Starling model:
options: ΔP_a ≈ 10 mmHg
ΔP_v ≈ 25 mmHg
Δπ ≈ 25 mmHg
At the venular end, water returns from the interstitial medium to the plasma
At the venular end, ΔP_v > Δπ
questions.explanation: Normal values: ΔP_a ≈ 40 mmHg, ΔP_v ≈ 10 mmHg, Δπ ≈ 25 mmHg. At the venular end Δπ > ΔP_v, so water goes back from the interstitial medium to the plasma; 25 mmHg is Δπ, not ΔP_v.

questions.stem: Under normal conditions (ΔP_a ≈ 40 mmHg, Δπ ≈ 25 mmHg), with L = 10⁻¹¹ m²·s/kg and 1 mmHg ≈ 133 Pa, the net water flux at the arteriolar end of the capillary is about:
options: 2×10⁻⁸ m/s, from the plasma to the interstitial medium
2×10⁻⁸ m/s, from the interstitial medium to the plasma
questions.explanation: ΔP_a > Δπ, so J_net,a = L(ΔP_a − Δπ) = 10⁻¹¹ × 15 × 133 ≈ 2×10⁻⁸ m/s and water leaves the plasma. 1.5×10⁻¹⁰ forgets the mmHg → Pa conversion; 8.6×10⁻⁸ adds the pressures instead of subtracting.
questions.mental: 40 − 25 = 15 mmHg ≈ 15 × 133 ≈ 2 000 Pa; × 10⁻¹¹ = 2×10⁻⁸ m/s. Direction: the bigger force at the arteriolar end is ΔP_a, so water goes out — this already removes B.

questions.stem: In the Starling model, the condition J_net,a = J_net,v (no water accumulation) leads to:
options: Δπ = (ΔP_a + ΔP_v) / 2, the mean pressure difference
Δπ = ΔP_a − ΔP_v
ΔP_a − Δπ = Δπ − ΔP_v
With ΔP_a = 40 mmHg and ΔP_v = 10 mmHg, it is satisfied for Δπ ≈ 30 mmHg
Δπ = ΔP_a + ΔP_v
questions.explanation: J_net,a = L(ΔP_a − Δπ) and J_net,v = L(Δπ − ΔP_v); equating them gives Δπ = (ΔP_a + ΔP_v)/2. With 40 and 10 mmHg this is 25 mmHg, not 30 (30 is the difference).

questions.stem: In a capillary, ΔP_a − Δπ > Δπ − ΔP_v. Then:
options: Δπ is lower than the mean pressure difference (ΔP_a + ΔP_v)/2
Δπ is higher than the mean pressure difference (ΔP_a + ΔP_v)/2
The extravascular medium is hyperhydrated: edema
The extravascular medium is dehydrated
More water leaves the plasma at the arteriolar end than returns at the venular end
questions.explanation: ΔP_a − Δπ > Δπ − ΔP_v means J_net,a > J_net,v and Δπ < ΔP̄: water accumulates outside the vessels, i.e. edema. Dehydration of the extravascular medium is the opposite case, Δπ > ΔP̄.

questions.stem: A patient has P_a = 50 mmHg and P_v = 20 mmHg (P_int = 0 as reference) and Δπ = 25 mmHg. According to the Starling model:
options: The mean pressure difference ΔP̄ = 30 mmHg
The mean pressure difference ΔP̄ = 35 mmHg
At the arteriolar end, the driving pressure of the net water flux is 25 mmHg
The extravascular medium becomes dehydrated
Edema forms
questions.explanation: ΔP̄ = (50 + 20)/2 = 35 mmHg > Δπ = 25 mmHg, so edema forms. At the arteriolar end J_net,a = L(ΔP_a − Δπ) = L × 25 mmHg. 30 mmHg is the difference P_a − P_v, not the mean.
questions.mental: Mean of 50 and 20 is 35; compare with 25 → ΔP̄ > Δπ → edema, which already rules out D. Arteriolar driving pressure: 50 − 25 = 25.

questions.stem: A patient has a plasma albumin concentration of 20 g/L (M = 40 000 g/mol), P_a = 45 mmHg, P_v = 15 mmHg, P_int = 0, 37 °C. The capillary is impermeable to albumin only. Then:
options: Δπ ≈ 9.7 mmHg
At the venular end, water returns from the interstitial medium to the plasma
Water leaves the plasma at both ends of the capillary
ΔP̄ = 30 mmHg > Δπ, so edema forms
The reflection coefficient of the membrane for albumin is 0
questions.explanation: Δπ = (0.5 mol/m³)·RT ≈ 1 288 Pa ≈ 9.7 mmHg. Both P_a = 45 and P_v = 15 exceed Δπ, so water leaves the plasma at both ends, and ΔP̄ = 30 mmHg > Δπ → edema. σ(albumin) = 1 since the wall is impermeable to it.
questions.mental: 20/40 000 = 0.5 mol/m³; RT ≈ 2 600 Pa, so Δπ ≈ 1 300 Pa ≈ 1 300/133 ≈ 10 mmHg. P_v = 15 > 10 settles the venular direction; (45 + 15)/2 = 30.

questions.stem: The figure shows the two forces acting on water at the arteriolar end of a capillary, under normal conditions (Starling model). About it:
options: The ΔP arrow represents the hydrostatic pressure difference pushing water from the plasma to the interstitial medium
The Δπ arrow represents the osmotic pressure difference drawing water from the interstitial medium into the plasma
At this end ΔP_a > Δπ, so the net water flux goes from the plasma to the interstitial medium
At this end J_net,a = L(Δπ − ΔP_a)
At this end Δπ is about 40 mmHg
questions.explanation: ΔP pushes water out of the plasma, Δπ (plasma proteins) pulls it back. At the arteriolar end ΔP_a ≈ 40 mmHg > Δπ ≈ 25 mmHg, so J_net,a = L(ΔP_a − Δπ) points toward the interstitial medium; 40 mmHg is ΔP_a, not Δπ.

questions.stem: In the Starling exercise of the lesson, the pressure units are related by 1 mmHg =
options: 133 Pa
1.36 cmH₂O
13.6 cmH₂O
760 Pa
questions.explanation: The lesson converts 1 mmHg = 1.36 cmH₂O = 133 Pa. 13.6 cmH₂O and 1.33 Pa are off by a factor of 10 and 100; 760 relates mmHg to the atmosphere, not to Pa.
